questions.explanation: A fast train cuts the travel time from Town F to City M. That could lead a bigger share of Town F's workers to take jobs in City M. If the share reaches 25%, Town F would meet this map's rule for being inside the commuting region.

questions.stem: Maps of "the Middle East" made by different governments, news organizations, and textbooks often include different sets of countries. Which statement best explains this?

options.A: The region has one official boundary, but some organizations use outdated maps
options.B: The region is organized around trade flows to a single central city
options.C: People define regions using different criteria, so boundaries can be contested
options.D: The maps use different projections, which change which countries appear in a region
options.E: The region has no shared characteristics, so it cannot be mapped consistently

rationales.A: Incorrect. There is no single, universally accepted boundary of the Middle East; organizations use different defining criteria.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The region is not defined by flows to one central city; the question is about the different criteria used to choose its countries.
rationales.C: Correct. Regions are defined by people using one or more chosen characteristics. Because organizations use different criteria, such as culture, history, or politics, regional boundaries are often contested and overlapping.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A map projection changes the shape and size of places, not which countries a mapmaker chooses to include in a region.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The countries share characteristics that many people use to define a region; the disagreement is over which countries meet the chosen criteria.

questions.explanation: People make regions by choosing what ties places together, like language, religion, history, or politics. Different groups choose differently, so their maps include different countries. That is why regional boundaries are often argued over and can overlap.

questions.stem: A subway map shows each line as a straight colored path with evenly spaced stations, even though the real tracks curve and the stations are different distances apart. Which statement best explains why the mapmaker drew it this way?

options.A: The mapmaker lacked accurate GPS data on the location of each station
options.B: Subway maps are reference maps, which require exact distances and shapes
options.C: The map is an isoline map that connects stations with equal numbers of riders
options.D: Map projections badly distort shape and area on maps of small areas such as a city
options.E: All maps are selective, and this one trades true distance for clear connections

rationales.A: Incorrect. The simplification is a deliberate design choice; accurate location data are easy to obtain, and the map leaves them out on purpose.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Reference maps help users locate places, but no map shows everything exactly; this map deliberately gives up true distance.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Isoline maps connect points of equal value on a continuous surface; subway lines connect stations along a route.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Straightening the routes and spacing the stations evenly are design choices; projection distortion does not explain that pattern.
rationales.E: Correct. All maps are selective in the information they show. A transit map gives up accurate distance and shape to make routes, transfers, and the order of stations easy to read.

questions.explanation: Every map leaves things out or changes things on purpose. A subway rider needs to know the order of the stops and where to switch lines, not the exact curve of the tracks. So the mapmaker straightened the lines to make the map easy to use.

questions.stem: A study combines national internet-access data to calculate one rate for Southeast Asia as a whole, then compares that rate with rates for other world regions. At which scale are the compared data aggregated (grouped)?

options.A: Global, because the regions being compared cover much of the world
options.B: Regional, because each compared value summarizes a world region
options.C: National, because the original figures came from individual countries
options.D: Local, because internet access can be measured for individual households
options.E: Global, because the internet connects places throughout the world

rationales.A: Incorrect. Comparing regions from across the world does not make each compared value a worldwide total.
rationales.B: Correct. The study combines country figures into one value for each world region, so the compared data are aggregated at the regional scale.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The original figures came from countries, but the study combines them into regional values before comparing.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Household information was combined into regional rates; individual household values are not compared.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The worldwide reach of the internet does not decide the level at which the data are grouped.

questions.explanation: The researchers make one number for Southeast Asia and compare it with one number for each other world region. So the compared data are regional, even though the original figures came from countries.

questions.stem: Between two censuses, State A's population grew much faster than the U.S. population as a whole, while State B's population stayed about the same. Based on the new census data, which outcome is most likely?

options.A: State A is likely to lose seats in the U.S. Senate, and State B may gain one
options.B: Both states keep the same number of House seats, since the number of seats per state is fixed
options.C: State A's boundary expands to include part of a neighboring state
options.D: State A may gain House seats, and State B may lose one if its population share falls
options.E: State B is likely to gain House seats to make up for its slower growth

rationales.A: Incorrect. Every state has two senators regardless of population, so census results do not change Senate seats.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The total of 435 House seats is set by law, but how those seats are divided among the states is recalculated after every census.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Census data can change representation and guide redistricting, but they do not redraw state boundaries.
rationales.D: Correct. After each decennial census, the 435 House seats are reapportioned using state populations and a set formula. Growing faster than other states can produce a seat gain, and a falling share can cost a seat, but growth does not guarantee a change.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Seats follow population; a state that grows slowly compared with the country tends to lose seats, not gain them.

questions.explanation: The census helps divide the 435 House seats among the states. A state whose share of the U.S. population goes up may gain a seat, and a state whose share goes down may lose one. A state can also keep the same number of seats.

questions.stem: Engineers in two countries on opposite sides of the world work on the same design in real time using video calls and shared online files. This situation best illustrates

options.A: time-space compression, because technology reduces the effect of distance
options.B: distance decay, because the engineers interact less as the distance between them grows
options.C: absolute distance, because the two countries are now closer together
options.D: a functional region centered on the engineers' main office
options.E: a formal region, because the engineers share the same profession

rationales.A: Correct. Time-space compression is the reduced importance of distance as transportation and communication technologies speed the movement of people, goods, and information. Real-time collaboration across the world is an example.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Distance decay predicts less interaction with greater distance; here the engineers interact closely despite great distance, which shows distance decay being weakened.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The absolute distance between the countries has not changed; what changed is how much that distance limits interaction.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the scenario describes a central office drawing in flows; it describes distance mattering less.
rationales.E: Incorrect. A shared profession could help define a formal region, but the scenario is about technology overcoming distance, not about a region.

questions.explanation: Time-space compression means the world feels smaller because technology lets people connect quickly over long distances. Video calls let engineers on opposite sides of Earth work together as if they were in the same room.

questions.stem: A popular navigation app uses real-time traffic data to send drivers off a jammed highway onto quiet residential streets. Which outcome is the most likely geographic effect of this decision?

options.A: The absolute distance between the highway and the neighborhoods will shrink
options.B: The residential streets will become a formal region defined by app use
options.C: The neighborhoods' relative location will change, since they are now farther from the highway
options.D: More cars will use residential streets, and towns may add speed bumps
options.E: Stores along the highway will move to the side streets to follow the traffic

rationales.A: Incorrect. Absolute distance does not change; rerouting changes travel time and traffic patterns, not the distance between places.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The scenario describes changed traffic flows, not an area defined by a shared, uniform trait.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rerouting does not move the neighborhoods farther from the highway. Their traffic connections may change, but the claim that they are farther away is unsupported.
rationales.D: Correct. Decisions made with geospatial data have geographic effects. Rerouting many drivers onto local streets increases traffic there, which can lead towns to lower speed limits, add speed bumps, or restrict turns.
rationales.E: Incorrect. A short detour around a traffic jam gives stores no reason to move; the direct, likely effect is more cars on the side streets.

questions.explanation: When the app sends lots of drivers onto small neighborhood streets, those streets get busy. Towns may then add speed bumps or new rules. A decision made with map data changed what happens on the ground.

questions.stem: On a map of the languages spoken at home in a border area, the share of people who speak Language X falls gradually from 90 percent to 10 percent over about 50 kilometers, with many bilingual towns in between. Which statement best describes the boundary of the Language X region?

options.A: It is a sharp line that follows the international border
options.B: It is a functional boundary based on travel to one city
options.C: It is a perceptual boundary, since the language people speak cannot be measured
options.D: It is set by law, so mapmakers place it in the same spot
options.E: It is a transition zone where the region blends into its neighbor

rationales.A: Incorrect. The share of Language X speakers changes gradually across about 50 kilometers, so there is no single sharp line.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The region is defined by a shared trait, the language people speak, not by flows to a central city.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The language spoken at home can be measured with surveys or census data; this is a formal region based on a measurable trait.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The map shows where people use the language, not a legally defined language area; some countries do set language areas by law, but the gradual change in percentages here points to a transition zone.
rationales.E: Correct. Regional boundaries are often transitional. Here the Language X region fades into its neighbor across a zone of bilingual towns rather than ending at a sharp line.

questions.explanation: Regions often do not have sharp edges. As you travel across this border area, Language X becomes less and less common, and many towns speak two languages. That in-between area is a transition zone.

questions.stem: A town that depends on a nearby forest for timber decides to cut no more trees each year than the forest regrows and to replant the areas it harvests. Which concept does this policy best reflect?

options.A: Environmental determinism, because the forest controls the town's economy
options.B: Sustainability, because it meets today's needs without using up the forest
options.C: Nonrenewable resource use, because cut trees cannot be replaced
options.D: Distance decay, because the town relies on the forest closest to it
options.E: Resource depletion, because the town removes trees from the forest each year

rationales.A: Incorrect. The town made a deliberate choice about how much to harvest; environmental determinism holds that the environment controls human activity.
rationales.B: Correct. Sustainability means using resources to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Harvesting no more than regrows, and replanting, keeps the forest productive.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Trees are a renewable resource; they regrow, which is what makes this policy possible.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The forest is nearby, but the policy is about how much to harvest over time, not about how interaction changes with distance.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Harvesting a renewable resource does not deplete it when the harvest stays within the rate of regrowth.

questions.explanation: Sustainability means using what you need now while leaving enough for the future. Cutting only as many trees as grow back, and replanting, means the forest will still be there for people later.
